welcome

focus::flow is a personal agenda built around the timer, your actual workload, and the patterns you build over time. you do not need to configure every feature before using it. start with Today, Tasks, and Habits; the rest can become useful when you need it.

  • focus tasks vs todos — focus tasks are work you may run the timer against. todos are quick items that do not need a focus session. you can switch a task between the two from its details.
  • today's focus range — adaptive mode starts from the median of your recent active focus days and adjusts gently for recovery, labour load, and whole-body fatigue. manual mode keeps the center fixed until you change it.
  • timer chain — the repeating pattern under the main timer: focus sessions, short breaks, then a longer rest. edit the counts and durations under the timer.
  • today's schedule — timed tasks can place themselves on the agenda when you start them. the timeline below can also be used to move and resize blocks.
  • habits — habits can have daily counts and weekly frequency targets. a task can also be linked to a habit so completing the task checks the habit automatically when appropriate.
  • goals — begin with a simple direction. optional structure such as why it matters, an obstacle, and a fallback plan can be added later. goals can sit in now, next, or someday and can link to tasks or habits for automatic progress.
  • recovery — enter the sleep, work, and fatigue information you have. You may leave fields empty. The app combines what is available and explains why it chose rest, easy, or harder training.
  • lifting — the app may choose one short lift that fits how tired you are. “Reps left” means how many clean repetitions you could still have done when you stopped.
  • books — books can be linked to reading tasks so focus time accumulates against the active book. notes, vocabulary, prompts, and review games stay attached to the book.
  • stats, reviews, and notes — Stats summarizes your own history rather than grading you against anyone else. daily check-ins, weekly recaps, and the floating notes pad are there when useful, not as requirements.

feature guide

Short explanations now appear beside the features that need them. This guide is the longer reference for what the app is calculating and what the controls actually do.
today, tasks & timer

focus task means the timer can be attached to it; todo means it is a quick item that does not need focus time. Current & next is the working queue, while Task Library is the reusable history of task names, time, notes, and usage.

adaptive focus range uses the median focus time from up to 28 recent active days once enough history exists. It then makes small adjustments for today's freshness, work hours × effort, and whole-body fatigue, and keeps the center between 30 and 180 minutes.

timer chain is the repeating sequence of focus sessions, short breaks, and the longer rest. Session presets on Tasks set a task-specific countdown; the main chain still controls the Pomodoro rhythm.

habits

Each habit can be a simple check-off, a count, minutes of duration, or something you are avoiding. Daily target and weekly frequency are separate. Partial progress is called a minimum kept so effort is visible even when the full target does not happen.

Linking a recurring task to a habit means completing that task can advance the habit automatically. Deleting a task card does not erase the saved task name/history from the library.

goals

now is active attention, next keeps something visible without making it urgent, and someday is a parking place you still want to keep in view. A title alone is enough to create a goal.

Why it matters, obstacle, and fallback plan are optional. Linking tasks or habits lets the goal use completed activity as progress, and periodic check-ins add your own behind / on-track / ahead judgment.

stats

sustainable daily capacity is the median focus minutes from your recent active days, not a maximum. consistency is the percentage of the last 30 days that contained focus time.

completion rate compares tasks completed with tasks completed plus tasks removed while unfinished. estimate accuracy compares actual task time with the timer estimate and reports whether you tend to finish over or under it.

personal patterns and the Recent interpretations are generated only from your own history, such as time-of-day, estimate bias, and session fragmentation. They are descriptive, not scores. History keeps longer charts and concrete milestones without streak bonuses or levels.

recovery & training call

recovery index is a 0–100 app estimate. It uses your HRV compared with your usual level, WHOOP recovery, sleep, how you feel, and whole-body fatigue. How you feel and whole-body fatigue count a little more than one sensor. The app reduces WHOOP’s weight when HRV or sleep is also present, so the same information is not counted twice. Training load is shown separately. This is not a medical measurement.

training sessions keep lifting and cardio separate. A lift appears automatically when its exposure is logged; runs, rides, and rows come from Intervals.icu or from a manual session if they will not sync. Each session keeps its own load and session RPE. When an uploaded stream-rich file has no source load or RPE, Focus::Flow can estimate load from duration and recorded heart-rate reserve; adding RPE later replaces that lower-confidence estimate. The old daily load fallback is used only when no session-specific cardio load exists.

HRV needs at least five previous entries before the app colors it against your own 30-day baseline. If entering only one resting-HR method, HRV4Training’s morning reading is recommended because it shares the same repeatable check-in context. WHOOP’s overnight value remains available but builds a separate baseline and should not be alternated with the morning method. Resting HR is not yet weighted into the recovery index. WHOOP recovery and sleep use three broad bands; how-you-feel gives extra weight to your subjective read of the day.

load ratio is the 7-day average workout load divided by the 28-day average. The app treats roughly 0.8–1.3 as its normal zone, 0.5–0.79 / 1.31–1.5 as caution, and values below 0.5 or above 1.5 as high deviation.

training call is the app’s plain answer for what to do next: rest, easy, medium, or a fitness test. Sleep, how you feel, work, sore body areas, recent workouts, and weekly limits can make the answer easier. The six-day and three-medium-day limits apply only to cardio. Work makes you tired but never counts as a workout. Lifting is checked separately.

lifting

The lifting tab has no mandatory A/B/C split. It ranks your lift pool by time since exposure, estimated fatigue cost, local body-region fatigue, recent RIR, and today's training call, then offers at most one exposure that fits the fatigue budget.

training max (TM) is the current working number used to calculate prescribed weight; it does not have to equal your true 1RM. historical high is kept separately and never erased by a layoff. RIR means reps in reserve. The goal is to finish with several clean reps left rather than turn the minimum-dose lift into a max effort.

Four exposures at the same TM with 4+ final-set RIR nudge the TM upward automatically. If a lift goes untrained for a long time, its working TM also regresses conservatively: no TM loss for the first 28 days, about -5% at 29–56 days, -7.5% at 57–90 days, and -12.5% after 90 days. Days 15–28 use a lighter re-entry prescription without rewriting the TM. Every regression is logged, while the historical high remains available in records. With your 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10, 25, 35 and 45lb plates, smaller/upper-body lifts move by 2.5lb while larger lower-body/posterior lifts move by 5lb. Prescribed loads round to 2.5lb so the recommendation is actually loadable.

sleep & physical fatigue

sleep debt adds up the hours below your chosen nightly sleep target over the rolling 14-day window. sleep consistency looks at variation in sleep start and end times over the last 7 days and needs several entries before it is meaningful.

work stress is work hours × perceived work effort. whole-body fatigue (stored as systemic fatigue) means general physical heaviness or exhaustion that is not mainly one body region. It can protect the whole training day, while leg, back, and upper-body fatigue mainly help the lifting engine avoid expensive movements for a tired region.

books, reviews & data

Reading-linked tasks prompt for the active book when needed, then logged focus time can be associated with that book. Book notes, vocabulary, prompts, progress, and review games are stored with the book.

Export creates a local JSON backup of app state. Import validates the basic backup structure before applying it. Cloud sync is optional; when signed out, data remains in browser storage on this device.

Recovery and training features are planning aids based on the values you enter. They are not a diagnosis or a substitute for medical evaluation, especially when pain, illness, or injury is involved.

how the goals tab works

this form is built around a few things that are actually shown, in research, to help goals stick — not just organizing tips. here's what each part is doing and why.

1. be specific — and let it be hard
"get in shape" rarely happens. "run a 5k by june" usually does better, even though it's the harder-sounding one. across hundreds of studies, specific and challenging goals consistently beat vague or easy ones — vague goals give your brain nothing concrete to aim at, and easy goals don't pull much effort out of you either.
2. name the obstacle — don't just picture success
it's tempting to skip straight to imagining the win. but research on this specifically found that picturing success on its own can backfire — your brain gets a small hit of "done" just from imagining it, and that can actually lower your drive to go do it. naming a real obstacle ("I'm too tired after work," "I forget by the time I get home") is what makes the visualization part actually work instead of working against you.
3. decide your response now, not later
"if I get home too tired to run, then I'll just do a 10-minute walk instead of skipping" — deciding this in advance, before you're actually tired on the couch, is one of the most reliable findings in this research for closing the gap between intending to do something and actually doing it. in the moment, you're not deciding anymore — you already decided.
4. the "why" is what gets you through a bad week
optional, but worth filling in. "I want to keep up with my kids" holds up better under a rough week than the goal title alone does.
5. link tasks or habits, and actually check in
link a goal to the tasks or habits that move it, and its progress bar fills in on its own — no manual updating. the occasional "behind / on track / ahead" prompt exists because goals you're not getting any feedback on tend to quietly die. answering honestly, especially "behind," is what keeps it alive.

how Recovery works

1 · inputsSleep, HRV, feel, fatigue, work, health flags, cardio load, lifting and session responses.
→
2 · what it meansRecovery signs describe today. Body Battery shows the app’s estimate now and after today’s suggested plan. Neither is a medical measurement.
→
3 · what to doTraining Call suggests rest, easy, medium, or a test. The 7-day view shows possibilities, not promises.
Recovery signsThe app combines the information you entered. How you feel and whole-body fatigue count the most. Empty fields are ignored, not treated as perfect.
Body Battery · estimatedThe large battery estimates what you have left now. A second number estimates what may remain after the rest of today and the suggested training.
Training CallThe strongest warning can make the plan easier. Being sick, pain, severe fatigue, or a very hard workday can matter more than a decent overall number.
Training loadRecent means the last 7 days. Usual means the last 28 days. Comparing them gives context, but it cannot prove that training is safe or predict an injury. Cardio-only leaves out lifting and work.
7-day outlookThis is not a fixed plan. Each day shows what might fit if your recovery stays similar.
Deload riskLooks for several longer-term warning patterns agreeing. Low means no meaningful deload pattern is currently detected.
Automatic HR flagsCompare HR with your earlier sessions at similar pace or power. One flag is low-weight; repetition matters more.
What updates whenMorning data updates the daily picture. Work and training logs revise reserve and load. Longer-term cards need repeated history.

      avalanche or snowball?

      minimums first · extra only where allowed
      This is added after every entered minimum payment. Accounts without confirmed penalty-free extra payments receive only their minimum.
      highest interest first · usually cheapestAdd debt balances and rates.

      adaptive leg recovery reset

      comfort first · reassess second · never erases other stop signals
      waiting for leg fatigue
      Log leg fatigue in today’s numbers. When it is elevated, Focus::Flow will offer one short recovery option and record whether it actually changes how your legs feel.
      today’s doseNo reset is prescribed until leg fatigue is logged.
      what this can—and cannot—doThese tools may reduce soreness or stiffness. They do not reliably restore performance, cancel accumulated load, or prove that a workout is safe.
      after the reset · re-rate, don’t negotiateRate the same leg-fatigue feeling again. A better number is useful feedback, but it does not automatically upgrade today’s prescription.
      today’s plan stays in chargeTry one option, then rate your legs again. Feeling a little better does not automatically mean a workout is safe.
      what the research says and when to stop
      Foam rolling. It may slightly reduce soreness and improve movement. It has not been shown to fully restore performance. 2019 review.
      Compression boots. They may help soreness feel better, but evidence that they restore muscle performance is limited. 2024 review.
      Leg elevation. Research after exercise is limited. Treat it as a comfortable rest position, not a treatment that makes you ready to train. small study.
      Do not use compression boots over wounds or infection, or when a clinician or device guide says not to. Ask a clinician first if a blood clot may be possible, one leg is swollen for no clear reason, or you have significant blood-flow, heart, or nerve problems. Stop for pain, numbness, colour change, breathing trouble, or worsening symptoms.

      formulas, evidence and limits

      One activity, one method. Focus::Flow chooses the first usable method in this order: imported source load → source intensity → sport threshold (cycling power or running pace) → session RPE × minutes → recorded heart-rate reserve. It never adds those alternatives together for the same activity. Lifting remains a separate estimated strength-stress model.

      The recent/base ratio is a descriptive 7-day versus 28-day comparison, not an injury probability. The app’s large-session and ramp warnings are conservative personal heuristics. Impellizzeri et al. (2020) describe conceptual and statistical problems with using acute:chronic ratios as injury-prevention prescriptions. Load is therefore only one input beside symptoms, fatigue, sleep, work and session response.

      The broad ranges are based on the joint Dietitians of Canada / Academy / ACSM sports-nutrition position statement. Protein is shown as a daily range with familiar meal anchors; carbohydrate scales with the prescribed session. Exercise energy is a deliberately wide net estimate above ordinary living, not permission to under-eat or a calorie target.

      sources, safety and limitations

      Joint sports-nutrition position statement: broad daily carbohydrate needs scale from light to moderate and high training; protein generally spans 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day and is better spread through the day. IOC REDs consensus: persistent low energy availability can impair health and performance.

      Focus::Flow does not know food intake, lean mass, medical history, climate, sweat rate, gastrointestinal tolerance or a body-composition goal. Repeated “not enough,” appetite trouble, weight loss, illness, menstrual changes, injury or worsening performance deserves a qualified sports dietitian or clinician—not a tighter app target.

      Activity connection
      Connect once per browser/device. The first sync imports one recent year of useful summaries; later automatic syncs only check recent activity.
      Intervals.icu settingsnot connected
      Find it near the bottom of Intervals.icu Settings. Paste it once on this browser/device. It is excluded from Focus::Flow backups and cloud sync, so a different device needs its own one-time paste.
      not synced yet
      Auto-sync checks the newest 45 days when Focus::Flow opens and about every 30 minutes while it stays open. Clear + restart removes Activity data and immediately imports the newest 365 days.
      Clear activities empties Activity-page entries, uploaded detail files, activity responses and record curves without forgetting your API key. Automatic importing stays paused until you deliberately press resume + sync. Export a backup first if you may want the removed details later.
      what gets imported
      Newest 365 days of useful activity summaries: sport · duration · distance · training load · average/max heart rate · average/normalized power · pace/speed · cadence · elevation · efficiency/decoupling. All-time pace and power best-effort curves stay as compact record summaries, so old personal bests do not require every old activity row.
      best route for Zwift
      Zwift → Intervals.icu directly → Focus::Flow. In Intervals.icu Settings, connect Zwift and enable Virtual Ride / Virtual Run. Avoid also importing those same activities from Strava, then use rebuild imported history here once. For an older or failed activity, upload the original Zwift FIT file to Intervals.icu first.
      Activity files
      Create several brand-new activities from original files, add one session manually, or repair files onto rows that already exist. Every multi-file action previews before changing history.
      Manual Upload
      Create new activities from one or many files, or repair detailed files onto existing history.
      It enters Activity history and Recovery as cardio load, without touching synced activities.
      If load is blank and duration + RPE are present, Focus::Flow uses session-RPE (minutes × RPE) and scales it to an internal app-load estimate. The raw session-RPE load is kept in the activity detail.
      batch new activity import
      Choose several FIT, TCX, or GPX files to create brand-new Activity rows. Focus::Flow checks file identity, start time, sport, duration and distance for duplicates before anything is saved. Files missing a sport can be classified here.
      batch file repair · existing activities
      Choose original FIT, TCX, or GPX files. Focus::Flow previews every match and never silently crosses sport or calendar date. This repairs stored rows; it does not create several brand-new activities.
      Activity load calculation
      Focus::Flow keeps one comparable load number per activity and names exactly where it came from. It can maintain working thresholds automatically from recent performance evidence, while a manual value always remains available. TSS-style load is repeatable output-based stress—not a direct measurement of your physiological response.
      cycling FTP · watts
      Sync a ride with an Intervals threshold or a recent power curve.
      running critical speed · min/km
      A 5 km test helps, but is not required when several other best efforts are available.
      1 · source loadIntervals.icu load is preserved when present, including its own configured power-, pace-, HR- or imported source method.
      2 · power / paceConsistent output-based stress: bike uses normalized power and FTP; run uses pace and threshold pace. Local run estimates are not official rTSS because grade-normalized pace is unavailable.
      3 · session RPEYour whole-session response replaces a weaker fallback when there is no source or threshold-based external load.
      4 · HR reserveLast fallback for files with useful HR. It describes cardiovascular response and is less responsive to brief hard efforts.
      Add an FTP or threshold pace to enable transparent local calculations. Changes autosave and rebuild derived load without duplicating activities.
      Threshold refresh guidance will appear after activity evidence is available.
      Cycling TSS-style load = hours × (normalized power ÷ FTP)² × 100. Running pace-style load = hours × (average speed ÷ threshold speed)² × 100. The speed ratio is used internally for arithmetic; running is displayed as min/km pace. HR and RPE are response-based fallbacks and are never stacked on top. Official TrainingPeaks rTSS additionally needs normalized graded pace; Xert XSS additionally needs Xert’s Fitness Signature and MPA model.
      Curve maintenance
      Duration curves guide training better than a trophy list because they show which ability is current, stale, or missing. Focus::Flow suggests only one useful check at a time, and Recovery decides whether today is an appropriate quality window.
      why a check appearsThe newest comparable effort is older than that duration’s freshness guide, or no usable effort exists.
      if the result is worseIt becomes the latest checkpoint. It does not erase a better effort or demand an immediate retest.
      current curveThe maintenance curve uses the most recent 365 days. All-time records remain in Personal bests.
      what changes nextTrain from the current Recovery call. Older bests leave this curve naturally; recent trends and threshold decay can then lower the working estimate.

      Similar-effort library

      Training chart workspace
      One large chart at a time, with the result, useful direction, and a practical way to use it. These are training signals—not a medical conclusion or a substitute for comparing genuinely similar workouts.
      waiting for dataAt least three older and three recent comparable sessions are needed before Focus::Flow comments on adaptation.
      Hover, tap, or use arrow keys where offered to inspect exact values.
      Running pace and heart rate
      Faster pace at a similar heart rate is the useful direction.
      Sync runs with duration, distance, and average HR.
      How to read itHorizontal position is average HR: farther left means fewer beats per minute. Vertical position is average pace in min/km: higher means faster. The bright dot is your newest run; the thin line joins the older-half median to the recent-half median.
      What the percentage meansPace efficiency converts pace to speed for the calculation, then divides by average HR so improvement remains positive. Positive means the recent half produced more running speed per beat; negative means less. All visible running values remain min/km.
      Use it carefullyCompare similar easy or steady runs. Hills, heat, wind, surface, fatigue, stops and intervals can move a dot more than fitness. One dot or one negative period is context, not a verdict.
      Cycling power and heart rate
      More power at a similar heart rate is the useful direction.
      Sync rides with average power and heart rate.
      How to read itHorizontal position is average HR: farther left means fewer beats per minute. Vertical position is average cycling power: higher means more watts. The bright dot is your newest ride; the thin line joins the older-half median to the recent-half median.
      What the percentage meansWatts-per-heartbeat is average power divided by average HR. Positive means the recent half produced more watts per beat; negative means less. The subtitle prints both median power/HR pairs so the percentage can be traced back to the chart.
      Use it carefullyCompare like rides: indoor with indoor, steady with steady, and similar heat, cadence, duration and fatigue. Coasting, intervals and different terrain can move average power and HR for reasons unrelated to fitness.
      Heart-rate decoupling
      Lower drift during steady aerobic work is usually preferable.
      Sync activities that include decoupling.
      How to read itEach dot is one workout ordered oldest to newest. Positive drift means HR rose relative to pace or power in the later portion. Negative drift means that ratio fell; warming up, changing output, stops or sensor behaviour can cause it.
      What the bands meanThe symmetric bands use absolute drift: 0–3% stable, 3–5% mild, 5–8% notable, and above 8% high. They are coaching guides—not physiological zones or universal pass/fail limits.
      When it is usefulUse steady aerobic sessions of similar duration and conditions. Intervals, hills, heat, dehydration, cardiac lag and changing effort make workout-to-workout comparisons unreliable.
      Sustained effort trend
      Detected efforts from separate workouts are shown through time.
      Upload stream-rich activities to build this trend.
      What it showsThe strongest detected section in the chosen duration band from each usable workout.
      Useful directionFaster running pace or higher cycling power across genuinely similar efforts may indicate progress.
      What to doUse it to find a pattern or a stale duration—not to call every detected section a test. Recovery still decides whether a hard check is reasonable.
      Running · 8-week volume and efficiency
      Weekly distance bars; the line tracks pace per heartbeat where usable.
      Sync runs with duration and distance; heart rate adds the efficiency line.
      What it showsWeekly running kilometres beside the efficiency available from runs with heart rate.
      Useful directionVolume grows gradually while efficiency stays stable or improves and fatigue remains manageable.
      What to doUse several weeks, not one bar. Check the Running load guard before adding a longer run.
      Cycling · 8-week volume and efficiency
      Weekly distance bars; the line tracks watts per heartbeat where usable.
      Sync rides with distance; power and heart rate add the efficiency line.
      What it showsWeekly cycling distance beside watts per heartbeat from rides with useful power and HR.
      Useful directionMore watts per heartbeat across comparable rides, without a sharp recovery or load cost.
      What to doSeparate indoor and outdoor context mentally, and judge a multi-week pattern rather than one ride.
      Combined cardio · time and load
      Weekly hours are bars; the line tracks total cardio load without mixing kilometres across sports.
      Sync or log cardio sessions with duration and load.
      What it showsTotal cardio time alongside the app’s summed cardio load for each week.
      Useful directionA sustainable chronic base rises through repeatable weeks instead of isolated stress spikes.
      What to doUse this with Recovery and sport-specific volume; equal load numbers can come from very different sessions.

      selected range · logarithmic time axis
      Sync power activities to draw the curve.
      What it showsYour best mean cycling power at short, medium and long durations in the selected record range.
      Useful directionA higher curve means more sustained power. Improvements may be specific to only one duration range.
      What to doInspect stale durations, but only test one when Recovery supports hard work and the result can change training.
      Running pace-duration curve
      selected range · lower pace is faster
      Sync run pace curves to draw the curve.
      What it showsYour best available pace across standard running distances in the selected record range.
      Useful directionA lower pace number is faster. Improvement may appear first at short or long distances rather than everywhere.
      What to doHover for exact values and compare the same date range. Do not treat every point as a deliberate maximal test.
      Running critical speed and D′
      The two-parameter model needs at least two genuinely hard efforts at different durations.
      Sync or upload runs with best efforts between about 2 and 20 minutes.
      How to read itEach dot is a best effort. Elapsed time is horizontal; distance is vertical. The fitted line’s slope is critical speed: a steeper line means a faster sustainable boundary.
      What D′ meansD′ is the line’s distance intercept—the modelled finite distance available above critical speed. It is not a fuel tank measured directly, and a larger number is not automatically better.
      Use it carefullyThe model assumes the selected efforts are close to maximal and reasonably current. A 5 km test improves the long end, but two or more qualifying shorter distances can produce an early, lower-confidence estimate.
      Focus::Flow compares recent sessions with your own earlier data. Heat, terrain, fatigue, workout structure, sensors, and indoor/outdoor conditions can all move these numbers.
